Foundations: know what people find and what you stand for

Before you change a single profile, you need to see yourself the way a stranger does and decide what you want to be known for. This module walks you through a search audit of your own name, helps you write a clear value proposition, and helps you pick the one or two platforms that matter most for your goals, with safety settings in place before you go public.
What a personal brand is, and auditing what people find about you today

A **personal brand** is simply what people understand about you, your skills and your character when you are not in the room. You already have one. Your customers describe you to their friends, your former colleagues say things about you, and anyone who searches your name or opens your WhatsApp profile forms a picture in a few seconds. Personal branding means taking charge of that picture so that it is **true, clear and easy to find**.

It is not about pretending to be a celebrity or posting every day. A caterer in Enugu, a teacher looking for a school job in Abuja, a tailor in Ibadan and a nurse applying abroad all benefit from the same thing: when someone looks them up, they quickly see what she does, who she does it for, and some proof that she does it well.
A woman looking at a profile page on a screen
Your profile is often the first meeting a client or employer has with you, before any call or visit.
Why the search comes before the meeting

Think about how you choose a new hairdresser or a supplier. You ask for her number, then you look at her WhatsApp profile picture, her Status, maybe her Instagram page. If the picture is blurred, the name is just an emoji and there is no sign of her work, you hesitate. Clients, recruiters and partners do exactly the same to you. The good news is that most people in your field have not tidied their presence, so a little careful work helps you stand out.
Three parts of every personal brand
**Clarity:** a person can say in one sentence what you do and who you help.
**Consistency:** your name, photo and description match on every platform, so people know it is the same you.
**Credibility:** there is real evidence, such as photos of your work, results, certificates or words from satisfied clients.

Your **value proposition** is the reason a particular person should choose you. It answers three questions: **Who do you help? What problem do you solve or what result do you give? Why should they trust you?** When you can answer these in one sentence, every profile, bio and introduction becomes easier to write, because they all grow from the same root.

Most profiles fail this test because they describe a job title instead of a result. 'Fashion designer' tells me your job. 'I make well-fitted owambe outfits for plus-size women in Port Harcourt, delivered in 10 days' tells me if you are right for me.

For example, Halima is a bookkeeper in Kano who wants small shop owners as clients.

Short, medium and long versions

You will need your statement in different lengths. A **short** version of about 10 words fits a WhatsApp About line or Instagram name area. A **medium** version of one or two sentences fits an Instagram bio or a LinkedIn headline. A **long** version of a short paragraph fits a LinkedIn About section, a Facebook Page intro or how you introduce yourself in a meeting.
Short: 'Monthly bookkeeping for small shops in Kano.'
Medium: 'Bookkeeper helping Kano shop owners see their real profit every month.'
Long: the full sentence plus a line on how to start, for example 'Send me a WhatsApp message for a free 20-minute review of your records.'
Proof that counts

Proof does not need to be grand. Good proof is **specific and checkable**: photos of your actual work, a certificate with the issuing body's name, the number of clients served, a short message from a client who agreed to be quoted, or a before-and-after result. If you are just starting, offer two or three people a discounted service in exchange for honest feedback and permission to show the result.
Never inflate

Do not claim clients, results or qualifications you do not have. A client who discovers one false claim will doubt everything else, and in some fields, such as health or finance, false claims can also break professional rules.
If you do more than one thing

Many women run two or three income streams, for example teaching by day and selling skincare in the evening. You do not need to hide this, but each profile should lead with **one main message**. Choose the stream that matches your biggest goal for the next year and make it the headline. Mention the others lower down, or give a second business its own WhatsApp Business number or Instagram page. A profile that says 'teacher, caterer, POS agent, real estate, wigs' leaves the reader unsure what to contact you for, so she contacts nobody.
Test it on a stranger
Send your medium version to someone who does not know your work well and ask: 'From this, what do I do and who is it for?' If their answer matches what you meant, your statement works.

Safety basics before you go public

A public profile attracts customers but also scammers. Before you share your number or handle widely, protect the accounts themselves. Account takeover is a common fraud: someone tricks you into giving them a verification code, then messages your contacts asking for money in your name.
WhatsApp: go to Settings, Account, Two-step verification, and create a six-digit PIN. Add an email address so you can reset it.
Instagram, Facebook and LinkedIn: open security settings and turn on two-factor authentication, using an authenticator app or SMS.
Use a different strong password for each account, written somewhere safe or kept in a password manager.
Never share any verification or login code with anyone, even someone claiming to be from the app, a bank or a friend.
Check your data costs and time

Video-heavy platforms use more data than text-based ones. If data is costly for you, note that you can upload posts when you are on Wi-Fi, use the data saver options inside most apps, and prepare captions offline in your notes app. Time matters too. Be honest: if you can give one hour a week, pick one platform and keep it tidy. A profile that was updated last month looks alive; a page whose last post was two years ago can make people wonder if you are still in business.
Claim your name everywhere you might need it

Even on platforms you will not use yet, it can help to reserve the same username, for example @halimabooks, so nobody else takes it. Choose a handle that is short, easy to spell when said aloud, and free of numbers that look like birth years. Use the same one everywhere you can.
Your never-post list

Decide now what you will never post publicly: your home address, your children's school or uniform, your daily routine and live location, photos of ID cards, bank cards or BVN details, and travel plans before you return. Share a business area, such as 'Lekki Phase 1', instead of a house address.
This is about your goals
Your list may look different from your friend's. A consultant may happily share her city and office, while a woman selling from home may share only a pickup point. Choose what protects you.

Your profile photo and bio are the two things almost everyone sees, even people who never scroll further. On WhatsApp the photo appears as a small circle beside every message you send. On LinkedIn and Instagram it appears beside every comment. That small circle has to work hard, so it should show **your face clearly, looking friendly and capable**.
A smartphone taking a selfie
A modern smartphone and good daylight are enough for a professional profile photo.
A professional photo with your phone

**Light:** stand facing a window or go outside in the shade in the morning or late afternoon. Avoid harsh midday sun overhead and avoid standing with the window behind you, which turns your face dark.
**Background:** choose a plain wall, a tidy shelf, or your workspace if it is neat. Remove clutter, laundry and bright patterns.
**Framing:** hold the camera at eye level, about an arm's length away, or ask someone to take it. Show your head and the top of your shoulders, with your face filling much of the frame.
**Outfit:** wear what a client would expect to see you in at work. Plain colours usually work better than busy prints, and avoid colours that match your background.
**Expression:** a natural, relaxed smile and eyes looking at the lens. Take 20 or more shots and choose the best.
**Edit lightly:** crop to a square, brighten a little if needed. Avoid heavy beauty filters that change your face, because clients should recognise you when they meet you.

**LinkedIn** is a professional networking site owned by Microsoft. Recruiters, employers, NGOs and many business buyers use it to find and check people. A complete profile works like an online CV that never sleeps, plus a place to show your work. It is free to join; the paid Premium plan is optional and not needed for this course.
A person reviewing an online CV on a screen
A complete LinkedIn profile works like a CV that people can find and check at any time.
The sections, in the order to fill them
Fill your LinkedIn profile in this order
Photo and banner
Headline
About
Experience and education
Skills and Featured
Recommendations
Top sections are seen first, so finish them before the lower ones.

**Photo and background banner.** Use your profile photo from the last lesson. For the wide banner, a simple image of your work, your city skyline or a plain design with your positioning line is enough. Canva has free LinkedIn banner templates.
**Headline (up to 220 characters).** This appears under your name everywhere on LinkedIn. Do not leave it as only your job title. Use: role or skill, who you help, specialty or result.

**About (up to 2,600 characters).** Write in first person. Open with who you help and how, give two or three proof points, list your main services or strengths, and end with how to contact you. Short paragraphs read well on phones.
**Experience.** For each role, add 3 to 5 lines starting with action verbs (managed, trained, reduced, grew) and include numbers where true. Self-employment counts: list your business as an employer.
**Education, licences and certifications.** Add degrees, NYSC if relevant, and certificates with the issuing body's name.
**Skills.** Add the skills recruiters search for in your field and pin your top ones. Colleagues can endorse them.
**Featured.** Pin your best proof: a portfolio PDF, a post about a project, a link to your website or catalogue.
**Recommendations.** Ask two or three former managers, colleagues or clients to write a short recommendation about specific work.
Worked example: before and after LinkedIn headline and experience
For example, Kemi worked six years as a customer service officer at a Lagos bank and wants a customer experience role in a fintech company.
Before headline: 'Customer Service Officer at a bank'. It describes only her current title.
After headline: 'Customer Experience Specialist | Resolving complaints and improving service in banking | Training frontline teams'.
Before experience line: 'Responsible for attending to customers.'

After lines: 'Handled walk-in and phone complaints for a branch serving thousands of customers.' 'Trained 8 new staff on complaint handling.' 'Helped cut repeat complaints by building a simple tracking sheet.'
She only includes numbers she can stand behind, for example the 8 staff she personally trained.
Kemi's profile now matches the words fintech recruiters search for, such as customer experience and complaint resolution, and shows results instead of duties.
Small settings that matter
**Custom public URL:** in 'Edit public profile & URL' change the random letters to your name, for example linkedin.com/in/kemi-adebayo. Put it on your CV and email signature.
**Open to work:** lets recruiters know you are looking. You can choose to show it to recruiters only, or to everyone with a photo frame.
**Location and industry:** set them accurately so local recruiters find you.
**Contact info:** add a professional email address, not one from your school days.
A simple About section structure

Many people freeze at the About box. Use four short paragraphs. **Paragraph 1:** who you help and what changes for them, which is your long positioning statement. **Paragraph 2:** your background in two or three sentences, including years of experience and the sectors you know. **Paragraph 3:** three or four strengths or services as short lines. **Paragraph 4:** a clear next step, such as 'Message me here or email kemi@example.com'. The first two or three lines show before a reader taps 'see more', so put your strongest sentence first.

If you are returning to work after a break, for example after raising children, you do not need to hide it. A short line such as 'Returned to the workforce in 2025 after a career break, during which I managed my family's provision shop' is honest and shows real skills. If you are a student or new graduate, lead with projects, NYSC service, volunteering and certificates.
Write first, paste later
Draft your headline and About in your notes app offline, count the characters, and paste them in when you have data or Wi-Fi. This saves data and gives you time to check spelling.
Be accurate about dates and titles
Employers often check references. Make job titles, dates and qualifications match your CV and certificates exactly. A mismatch can cost you an offer.

WhatsApp Business: the essentials
WhatsApp Business is a free app from WhatsApp for small businesses. You can run it on a separate number from your personal WhatsApp. Its tools include:
**Business profile:** business name, category, description, address or service area, business hours, email and website.
**Catalogue:** add products or services with photos, prices and descriptions so customers can browse without asking 'how much?' each time.
**Greeting message:** an automatic reply the first time someone messages you, for example welcoming them and sharing your catalogue.
**Away message:** an automatic reply outside your business hours.
**Quick replies:** saved answers you insert by typing a shortcut, useful for prices, account details and delivery terms.
**Labels:** tag chats such as 'New order', 'Paid', 'Delivered' to keep track, so no paid order is forgotten in a busy week.
Instagram: professional account

Consistency matters more than volume. Posting twice a week for six months builds more trust than posting every day for two weeks and then vanishing. Pick a rhythm you can keep even in a busy month. **Value:** two to five short lines that teach, show or prove something specific.

**Next step:** tell people what to do, such as 'Save this', 'Ask me in the comments' or 'Book via the WhatsApp link in my bio'.

Scams that target visible people
**Code theft:** a message, often from a friend's hacked account, asks you to forward a code 'sent by mistake'. It is your login code. Never share it.
**Fake support or verification:** messages claiming your page will be deleted unless you log in through a link, or offering a 'verified badge' for a fee. Check only inside the app's own settings.
**Impersonation:** someone copies your name and photo and asks your customers for payment. Warn customers on Status that you only use one number, and report the fake account in the app.
**Fake payment alerts:** screenshots or SMS that look like credit alerts. Confirm in your own bank or wallet app.
**Overpayment refunds:** a 'customer' sends too much and asks for the extra back. Wait until the money truly arrives, and be suspicious.

Ethics: honesty and permission

Ethical branding rests on two habits. First, **say only what is true**: real qualifications, real results, real reviews. Second, **ask before you share** anything about another person. A client's name, face, house, chat screenshot or result belongs to them. Ask in writing, for example: 'May I share a photo of your finished dress and your review on my Instagram? I can hide your name if you prefer.' Keep their reply.
Worked example: sharing a review the right way
For example, Bisi is an interior decorator in Ibadan. A client sends a happy voice note and photos of her finished living room.
Bisi replies: 'Thank you so much. May I share two photos of the room and a written line from your message on my page? I will not show your house front, street or family photos.'
The client agrees but asks that her name is not used.
Bisi crops out a family portrait and a window that shows the street.
She posts: 'Living room refresh, Ibadan. Client said: "You understood exactly what I wanted."' with no name.
She screenshots the permission message and saves it in a folder called 'Permissions'.
Bisi gains strong proof for her profile while protecting her client's privacy and keeping a record of consent.
Customer data and the law

Nigeria has the **Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023**, overseen by the **Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC)**. In simple terms, it expects people and businesses that collect personal information to collect only what they need, use it for the purpose they gave, keep it secure and respect people's rights over their data. For a small business this means: do not add customers to broadcast lists or groups without their agreement, do not share their numbers with others, and delete records you no longer need.
Handling negative comments

A visible profile will sometimes attract complaints or rude comments. Reply calmly and briefly in public, then move the details to a private chat, for example: 'Sorry about this experience. Please send me a message so I can sort it out today.' Do not argue in public, and do not delete fair complaints, because how you respond is itself proof of your professionalism. You can block or report accounts that post abuse or threats.
Delay location posts
Post photos from events, travel or a client's site after you have left, not live. This protects you and the people you work with.
When in doubt, leave it out
If you are not sure whether a post could embarrass a client, reveal private information or be seen as a false claim, do not post it. You can always ask first.

**Networking** is building genuine relationships with people who can learn from you, work with you or introduce you to others. Online networking follows the same rules as networking at a wedding or a conference: introduce yourself politely, show interest in the other person, offer value before asking for anything, and follow up. The most common mistake is the opposite: sending a stranger 'Hi dear, please patronise me' or a long sales message before any relationship exists.

Networking online lets you meet clients, mentors and employers far beyond your street or city.
Who to connect with
**Peers:** people doing similar work, who can share knowledge and refer overflow jobs.
**Potential clients or employers:** the people your positioning statement names.
**Connectors:** event organisers, association leaders, community managers and journalists who know many people.
**Mentors:** people a few steps ahead of you, whose path you would like to follow.

Writing a connection request

On LinkedIn, add a short note when you can. Free accounts may be limited in how many personalised notes they can send each month, so use them for people who matter most. A good note says how you know of them, one specific thing you appreciate, and why you would like to connect. No sales pitch.
Worked example: before and after connection request
For example, Kemi, now targeting customer experience roles, wants to connect with a customer experience manager at a fintech company she follows.
Before: 'Hello ma, please I need a job in your company. Kindly help.' It asks a stranger for a big favour immediately.
She first follows the manager and reads her recent posts for two weeks.
She leaves one thoughtful comment on a post about complaint handling, adding her own experience in two sentences.

After note: 'Good afternoon, I enjoyed your post on reducing repeat complaints. I have spent six years in bank customer service and am moving into fintech CX. I would value connecting and learning from your work.'
A month later, after another useful exchange, she asks: 'Would you be open to a 15-minute chat about how your team hires?'
The manager accepts, recognises Kemi's name from the comment, and agrees to a short call. Kemi gets advice and an introduction to the recruiter, without ever sending a pushy request.
Comments that build your name

A thoughtful comment on someone else's post can be seen by their whole audience. 'Nice one' or 'Congratulations' adds nothing. Instead, add a short experience, a useful tip or a good question. For example, on a post about catering for large events: 'We found that labelling each cooler with the serving time cut food waste a lot at a 300-guest wedding. Do you plan portions per head or per table?'
Groups and communities

Join a few active groups where your audience gathers: professional associations, alumni groups, LinkedIn groups in your field, Facebook groups for your city or trade, and WhatsApp communities. Read the rules first. Many groups ban adverts except on certain days. Become known for helpful answers, and people will check your profile on their own.

If there is no reply after two polite follow-ups, move on graciously.

Real employers do not charge applicants to be hired. Meet new business contacts in public places or by video call first, and tell someone where you are going.

Adding new contacts to your sales group or broadcast list without consent annoys people, can get your number reported, and goes against good data practice. Ask first, and give an easy way to leave.

Explaining your value

When someone asks 'What do you do?' or an interviewer asks about your skills, use a short spoken pitch of about 30 seconds built from your positioning statement and one result. Pattern: **who you help, what you do, one result, an invitation.** For example: 'I help small shop owners in Kano see their real profit each month. Last quarter one pharmacy client found it was losing money on two product lines and dropped them. If you run a shop, I can do a free 20-minute review of your records.'
Adapting the pitch to the listener
**To a potential client:** lead with the problem you solve for people like them, then one result, then an easy next step such as a free sample, consultation or price list.
**To an interviewer:** lead with your skill area and years of experience, give one specific achievement with a number you can defend, and link it to the job you are applying for.
**To a peer or connector:** say who your ideal client is, so they know whom to refer to you, for example 'If you meet shop owners who struggle with records, please send them my way.'

Practise until it sounds natural, not memorised. Record yourself on your phone, listen back, and cut any sentence that does not add information. Most people find their first version runs too long; aim for about 75 words, which takes around 30 seconds to say at a relaxed pace.

Your maintenance routine
**Weekly:** post to your rhythm, reply to messages and comments, update your enquiry log.
**Monthly:** review numbers, update prices and catalogue, ask for at least one testimonial, check that links work.

**Every three months:** reread your positioning statement, refresh your Featured and Highlights with recent work, check privacy settings, remove outdated prices or services, and update your 'after' screenshots so your record shows steady progress.
**Yearly or when your look changes:** new profile photo across all platforms.
When to change your positioning

Do not rewrite your brand every month. Consider a change when your evidence points to it: most of your paid work comes from a different type of client than you expected, you have gained a new qualification, or your goal has changed, for example from selling products to training other women. When you change, update every platform on the same day, so your presence stays consistent, and keep the old screenshots as part of your record.

The most common mistake is a stranger getting a message like: Hello ma, please I need a job in your company. It asks for a big favour before any relationship exists.

For example, Kemi wants to move into customer experience at a fintech company. She follows a manager there and reads her posts for two weeks, then leaves one thoughtful comment from her own experience.
Her note names the post she enjoyed, her six years in bank customer service, and asks only to connect. A month later she asks for a 15-minute chat, and the manager says yes.

Three warning signs
Real employers do not charge applicants to be hired.
Meet new contacts in public or by video call first, and tell someone where you are going.
Never add people to your groups or broadcasts without asking. Give an easy way to leave.
Not every friendly contact is genuine. Be careful with anyone who quickly moves to money or asks for an upfront processing fee for a job. Real employers do not charge applicants to be hired.
Never let anyone push you to meet alone at a private address. Meet in public or by video call first, and tell someone where you are going.
And on your side, never add new contacts to your sales group or broadcast list without asking. After two polite follow-ups with no reply, move on graciously.

Your work portfolio needs three to six strong, recent pieces. For each, say what the client needed, what you did and the result. Then prepare a short spoken pitch.
Halima says: I help small shop owners in Kano see their real profit each month.
Last quarter, one pharmacy client found it was losing money on two product lines and dropped them.
If you run a shop, I can do a free 20-minute review of your records.
Aim for about 75 words. Only claim results you directly caused or contributed to.
Your 90-day plan
Blessing's plan with dates
Keep three targets at most, and set them from your own numbers.
A brand stays strong with a simple routine and a plan with dates. For example, Blessing, the Benin City hairstylist, starts from her log: about 12 new WhatsApp enquiries a month, 3 from Instagram.
In days 1 to 30 she fixes gaps. Her target is 5 written client reviews, with permission, by day 30.
In days 31 to 60 she keeps posting and connects with 15 salon owners or managers on LinkedIn.
By day 90 she aims for 18 enquiries a month, at least 6 from Instagram. Become famous is not a target. A number you can count is.
